questions.q: Why does this lesson say a portfolio substitutes for a missing standardized certification in quantum computing hiring?
options: With no dominant standardized credential, hiring leans on direct evidence of capability -- real project work, which is a fairer but more demanding test
Because certifications are forbidden in the quantum computing industry
Because portfolios are easier to fake than certification exams
Because quantum computing companies never check any credentials at all
questions.explain: The lesson explains that without a dominant standardized credential like CompTIA or AWS certifications, direct project evidence does the work -- a fairer test of real ability, but one where the burden of producing convincing evidence falls on the candidate.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say this course's capstone specifically adds value beyond a toy project like 'I implemented Grover's algorithm'?
options: It demonstrates research-adjacent skills -- hypothesis formation, controlled comparison, honest handling of discrepancies -- that a simple implementation project doesn't show
Because toy implementation projects are no longer accepted by any employer
Because the capstone requires no actual quantum computing knowledge
Because Grover's algorithm is considered obsolete
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts the capstone's research-skill demonstration (hypothesis, controls, honest discrepancy handling) with a simpler implementation-only project.

questions.q: What makes the resume bullet 'Reproduced a published zero-noise-extrapolation result... and diagnosed a calibration-window confound' stronger than 'Explored quantum error mitigation,' per this lesson?
options: It names the specific technique, specific result, and specific tools/judgment demonstrated, rather than a vague skill-area description
It is shorter and therefore easier to read
It avoids mentioning any specific hardware
It uses more technical jargon, which the lesson says is always preferred
questions.explain: The lesson's standard for resume bullets is specificity -- naming the exact technique, result, and tools -- which the stronger example does and the vague one does not.

questions.q: How does the lesson say vendor-recognized completions (IBM Quantum, Microsoft Learn) should be treated relative to project portfolio work?
options: As a supplement to the portfolio, not a substitute -- they show learning-path completion, not independent experiment design and reporting ability
As the single most important credential, more valuable than any project
As completely irrelevant and not worth listing at all
As a full replacement for the capstone project
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that these completions are worth listing as a supplement, but they demonstrate completing a learning path, not the independent design/execution/reporting skill the project work and capstone actually prove.

questions.q: In the worked portfolio-to-resume translation, how many distinct hireable signals does the lesson say the single capstone resume bullet demonstrates?
options: Four -- experimental design, hands-on hardware experience, research-integrity judgment, and communication skills
One -- only technical hardware experience
Zero -- the bullet is considered too vague to be useful
Two -- only coding ability and writing ability
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly counts four distinct signals from the one well-described bullet: experimental design, hands-on hardware experience, the confound-diagnosis judgment, and communication skills from the reports/presentations.
